description: What AR is, the five sectors that use it, three types of AR, and the devices that bring it to life.
hero_image_caption: A person using a mobile device to view an augmented reality overlay in real space.
content_html:
What is Augmented Reality?

Augmented reality (AR) adds a digital layer on top of the physical world. Unlike virtual reality, which replaces your surroundings entirely, AR keeps the real world visible and places digital objects within it. A user pointing a device at a shelf in a shop might see a product’s nutritional information appear floating above the packet — that is AR in action.

AR relies on a device’s camera to capture the real environment, software to process that image, and a display to overlay the digital layer. The result is a combined view that gives users more information or interaction than the physical world alone can provide.

Key Fact

AR overlays digital content onto the real world. Virtual reality replaces the real world entirely. The key word for AR is “overlay” — reality is still visible.

Sectors That Use AR

AR is used across five key sectors, each exploiting the technology in different ways to meet the needs of their audience.

In architecture, AR allows architects and clients to view a 3D model of a proposed building placed inside its actual future location. Instead of reading a flat plan, a client can walk through an empty plot and see the building’s scale and appearance in context. This is an example of AR used for visualisation of designs.

In education, AR can overlay labels on anatomy models, bring historical events to life on a museum floor, or allow students to examine structures that would be impossible to view physically — such as the inside of a cell or a working engine. This supports understanding through interactive engagement.

In entertainment, AR is used in location-based gaming where digital characters or items appear in real-world spaces. Theme parks use AR to make exhibits interactive, and live events use it to add visual effects that audience members can view through their devices.

In retail, AR is used for marketing and to let customers try products virtually. A customer browsing furniture can point their phone at a corner of the room to see how a sofa would look there before ordering. Cosmetics retailers use AR “try-on” tools so shoppers can preview make-up without physically applying it.

In the lifestyle sector, AR appears in fitness apps that overlay coaching cues onto a live camera feed, navigation apps that place directional arrows on the real street view ahead, and home improvement apps where users can visualise paint colours or wallpaper in their own rooms. Virtual tours fall into this category too — estate agents and tourist attractions increasingly use AR to let people explore spaces remotely.

Types of Augmented Reality

There are three distinct types of AR. Understanding which type is used in which context is an important part of both planning an AR product and answering extended-response questions.

Key Fact

The three types of AR are: marker-based (object recognition), markerless (location-based), and superimposed. Each uses a different method to decide where to place the digital layer.

Marker-based AR (also called object recognition AR) works by detecting a unique static image — the marker — through the device camera. When the marker is recognised, digital content is overlaid directly on top of it. Examples include product packaging that triggers a 3D animation when scanned, or printed posters that come to life when viewed through an app. The marker itself must be unique and clear — blurred images, too much text, or large areas of blank space all reduce the system’s ability to detect it reliably.

Markerless AR (location-based AR) does not rely on a specific trigger image. Instead, it uses the device’s sensors — GPS, accelerometer, or surface-detection technology — to understand its position and orientation in the real world, then places digital content relative to that position. Navigation apps that place arrows on the road ahead and AR games where characters appear in any outdoor environment use markerless AR.

Superimposed AR partially or completely replaces the view of a real object with a digitally altered version. Medical imaging software that overlays a scan on top of a patient’s body during a procedure, and furniture apps that replace a blank wall with a virtual wallpaper design, both use superimposed AR.

User Interaction: Static and Interactive Layers

Once an AR product is triggered, the user can experience it in one of two ways. A static layer simply presents information — the user reads or watches but cannot interact further. An interactive layer responds to user input: the user might swipe, tap, click, or speak a command to reveal further content, navigate between layers, or control the AR experience. Interactive layers give users more control but require more complex design and testing.

Devices Used with AR

AR can be delivered on three types of device. Mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets are the most common: they have cameras, GPS, and sufficient processing power for most consumer AR applications, making them accessible to the widest audience. Smart devices include wearables such as AR glasses and smart headsets, which can overlay information without requiring the user to hold up a screen — useful in hands-free environments such as manufacturing or surgery. Laptops and desktop PCs can also run AR applications, especially those that use a webcam as the input and display AR content on-screen — common in design and education software.

Not every AR type suits every device. Marker-based AR works well on mobile devices where the user can point the camera at a marker. Markerless AR often requires GPS and motion sensors, which limits it to mobile devices or specialist wearables. Superimposed AR can run on any device with a camera capable of recognising the target object, including laptops.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to “describe” a type of AR, give the name and one defining feature — not just the name alone. For example: “Marker-based AR uses a unique static image as a trigger to overlay digital content.” If you only write “uses a marker” without explaining what the marker does, you are unlikely to earn the description mark. ‘Explain’ questions go further — they ask for reasons, so link the feature to a benefit using “because,” “therefore,” or “this means that.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • AR overlays digital content onto the real world; the five main sectors using it are architecture, education, entertainment, retail, and lifestyle.
  • The three types of AR — marker-based, markerless, and superimposed — each use a different trigger mechanism.
  • AR runs on mobile devices, smart devices, and laptops/PCs; the best device depends on the AR type and the user context.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of AR uses GPS to place digital content relative to the user's real-world position?
A. Marker-based AR
B. Markerless AR
C. Superimposed AR
D. Static AR
practice_questions.marks: B — Markerless AR. (1 mark for correct letter or full term.)

practice_questions.text: Identify one sector, other than retail, that uses AR.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for any one of: architecture / education / entertainment / lifestyle. Accept a named example that clearly identifies one of these sectors.

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by marker-based AR.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that marker-based AR uses a unique static image (1) and that when the camera detects this image, digital content is overlaid on or around it (1).
Secure: Names the use of a static image/trigger (1) with some indication of content appearing (1).
Developing: States only 'uses a marker' or 'uses a special image' with no further qualification (1 mark only).
Emerging: Vague or incorrect response (0).

practice_questions.text: Describe two uses of AR in the architecture sector.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per distinct use, up to 2 marks. Accept: visualising a proposed building in its real location / allowing clients to see a 3D model of a design before construction / virtual tours of unbuilt spaces / overlaying design plans onto a physical site. Each answer must describe a use, not just name a general category.

practice_questions.text: Explain why markerless AR is better suited to a mobile device than to a laptop. Use the word 'because' in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Identifies that markerless AR relies on GPS and motion sensors (1) AND states that mobile devices have built-in GPS and accelerometers whereas most laptops do not (1) AND links this to a user benefit such as being able to use the AR application outdoors while moving (1).
Secure (2): Two clear points with a reason connecting device features to AR requirements.
Developing (1): One point such as 'mobile devices have GPS' without connecting this to the needs of markerless AR.
Emerging (0): Vague or irrelevant response.

practice_questions.text: A school is planning to use AR in its science lessons to help students explore the structure of a human cell. Discuss whether marker-based or markerless AR would be more suitable for this purpose. You should consider the advantages and disadvantages of each type.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): Balanced discussion of both types with clear understanding of both. Marker-based: recognises a printed image of the cell and overlays 3D content — reliable in a classroom, easy to set up on a worksheet or textbook page, but students must have the marker present. Markerless: no fixed trigger needed, more flexible, but depends on surface detection and GPS which may be unreliable indoors / the school environment may not support it well. Reaches a justified conclusion that relates the chosen type to the school context (e.g. marker-based is more suitable because printed markers on worksheets are inexpensive and reliable in a classroom with no GPS requirement). Evidence embedded throughout.
Secure (5–7): Clear understanding of both types with relevant points about each. Some comparison. Conclusion present but may not be fully justified with reference to the school context.
Developing (3–4): Describes one type well or gives surface-level points about both. Limited comparison. Conclusion absent or unsupported.
Emerging (1–2): Some relevant knowledge of AR types but little application to the scenario. No comparison or conclusion.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of AR partially or entirely replaces the view of a real object with a digital version?
In which sector would AR most likely be used to allow a customer to see how a sofa would look in their home before buying?
AR overlays digital content onto the real world, unlike virtual reality which _____ it entirely.
A marker-based AR trigger must be _____ so that the device camera can reliably detect it.
Match each AR type to its key feature.
right: Uses GPS or surface detection — no fixed trigger
Partially or fully replaces the view of a real object
Detects a unique static image to trigger content

flashcard_questions.q: What does AR stand for and what does it do?
flashcard_questions.a: Augmented reality — overlays digital content onto the real world.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between AR and virtual reality?
flashcard_questions.a: AR keeps the real world visible; VR replaces it entirely.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the five sectors that use AR.
How is AR used in the architecture sector?
flashcard_questions.a: To visualise proposed designs in their real location before building.

flashcard_questions.q: How does marker-based AR know where to place content?
flashcard_questions.a: It detects a unique static image (the marker) through the camera.

flashcard_questions.q: How does markerless AR know where to place content?
flashcard_questions.a: It uses GPS or surface-detection sensors — no fixed trigger image.
Partially or entirely replaces the view of a real object with a digital version.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three types of devices AR can be used on.
What is a static AR layer?
flashcard_questions.a: A layer that presents information only — the user cannot interact with it.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an interactive AR layer?
flashcard_questions.a: A layer the user can control, e.g. by swiping, tapping or using voice.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a virtual tour in the context of AR?
flashcard_questions.a: A guided AR experience allowing users to explore a location digitally.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must a marker-based AR trigger be unique?
flashcard_questions.a: So the camera can distinguish it from other images and trigger the correct content.

glossary_terms.definition: A technology that overlays digital content — images, text, video or 3D objects — onto a live view of the real world.
Using AR to display a digital version of a design, product or space within its real-world environment before it is built or purchased.
Using AR to promote a product by allowing customers to interact with or preview it digitally before buying.
A guided AR experience that allows a user to explore a location digitally without being physically present.
A type of AR that recognises a unique static image or physical object as a trigger to overlay digital content.
A type of AR that scans the surrounding environment using sensors such as GPS, rather than recognising a fixed image trigger.
A type of AR that partially or entirely replaces the view of a real object with an augmented version of it.
